messages.content: [UFC at the White House perfectly fits the America of today -- love it or hate it] WASHINGTON -- A quick note to future historians who may find this dispatch -- hopefully, when the United States has already enjoyed its 350th or 500th or whatever anniversary. Yes, in honor of America's 250th, a seven-match Ultimate Fighting Championship card was staged on the grounds of the White House. Seriously. This was one of the ways 250 years of independence was celebrated. It was right there in the backyard, in a makeshift stadium with flashing lights, Octagon girls in stars-and-striped dresses and the 160-piece Marine Band playing the walkout music for fighters arriving from all parts of the White House, even the Oval Office. They were even serving Bud Lights. Again, seriously. This all happened on Sunday: Fight Night at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. After a rain delay and a flyover to start the festivities, the UFC Freedom 250 was spectacle for celebrities and politicians alike. Carolyn Van Houten for ESPN And yes, it was a preposterous idea; a combination of ludicrous logistics and wonderful ambition. It was a circus act of an event that managed to both thrill and enrage various segments of the populace, much like everything these days. The purple mountains might deliver the majesty, the fruited plains the amber waves of grain. The South Lawn, though, has its blood-splattered mat inside an eight-sided cage. Debate among yourselves which of the above best represents the current status of this wonderful nation of ours: America, the beautiful. There are many who loved this, many who despised this (and we'll get to both). The one undeniable truth is that the UFC put on a rollicking, raucous show in the most unlikely of locations: outside, in the humidity of Washington in June, at a facility built for governance, not sport. [Napoli president wants ultras out of any new stadium, warns Allegri] With two Serie A trophies in the last four years and five other domestic cups, Napoli president Aurelio De Laurentiis is proud of what he has accomplished since rescuing the club from bankruptcy and starting in Serie C more than two decades ago. Yet he also wants more. De Laurentiis discussed plans for a new stadium that he hopes would be more attractive to families by keeping out hard-core "ultra" fans and sent a warning to coach Massimiliano Allegri while collecting an award recognizing his career in sports at the Foreign Press Association on Wednesday. A film producer, De Laurentiis is one of the last Italian owners of Serie A's biggest clubs. Napoli currently play in the dilapidated Stadio Diego Armando Maradona, which is owned by the city and where sight lines are poor due to a running track. "I have a letter of intent signed a month ago by which in eastern Naples we've found 38 hectares (94 acres) where I've planned a 70,000-seat stadium with 120 sky boxes, plus restaurants and an interactive museum," De Laurentiis said. However, city officials have proposed renovating the Maradona stadium in time for the 2032 European Championship that Italy are co-hosting with Turkey. De Laurentiis has had issues with the "ultras" for years and most recently made an attempt to prevent the hard-core supporters from bringing banners inside the stadium. "Soccer should be about passion and participation. It has to be educational for kids. You can't have hooligans ... or 'ultras' that are moulded from the Mafia, 'ndrangheta and Camorra," De Laurentiis said, listing three of Italy's organized crime syndicates. "Until our police chiefs and government ministers get the situation under control it's a major problem."
